title: The Context-Rebuilding Tax at Brownfield Plants
summary: Every HAZOP, MOC, shutdown job, and investigation starts the same way: someone rebuilds plant context by hand. The cost never shows up as a line item — and it never goes away on its own.
body_text: The week before a HAZOP looks the same at most brownfield plants. The study leader pulls the P&IDs for the unit — scanned PDFs, a revision cloud from 2011 still sitting on sheet 4 — and starts building context by hand. Which safeguards protect this node? The safeguard list from the last study is nine years old. Did we ever have an incident on this type of exchanger? There was one, people think, in another unit, before the current team's time. Where is the relief valve datasheet? In a folder, somewhere, probably. None of this is analysis. It is retrieval — assembling facts that already exist in the plant's own documents so that the actual work can begin. And when the session finally runs, part of it goes to debating facts that were written down somewhere all along. The same tax on every workflow Call it the context-rebuilding tax . Every workflow at a brownfield plant pays it. A HAZOP starts with days of P&ID review and precedent hunting. An MOC review starts by finding the affected SOPs, interlocks, and past incidents — usually from memory. A shutdown work pack starts by reassembling the same equipment context that was assembled last shutdown, by someone else, who has since changed roles. An investigation starts with the timeline and the history hunt. A parts order starts with a 40-page scanned vendor datasheet and a planner's recollection of which model variant is actually installed. The tax is invisible because it hides inside other jobs. Nobody's timesheet says "context reassembly." It shows up as HAZOP prep, permit preparation, work-pack planning, investigation. And because it never appears as its own line item, it never becomes a project, never gets a budget, and never goes away on its own. "But we have a DMS" The plants that pay this tax most heavily are not short on systems. There is a DMS, an EAM, SharePoint, a historian, and folders of vendor documents. The documents exist. What does not exist is the connection between the documents and the place where work actually starts: the drawing . A process plant runs on its P&IDs. Isolation boundaries are traced on them. HAZOP nodes are marked on them. The permit references them. But in most brownfield sites the P&ID is a scan — a picture of plant intelligence, not the thing itself. You cannot click a pump on a picture. So every job begins with a person acting as the join between the drawing and the ten systems that hold its context. That person is usually senior. They are the ones who know where things are, which revision is current, and what happened on that line in 2014. Which means the most experienced engineers at the plant spend a real share of their week doing retrieval — the one part of the job that does not need their judgment. What it costs Three things, in increasing order of severity. Hours — mostly senior-engineer hours, paid again on every review, permit, shutdown job, and investigation. Variance — the quality of an isolation plan or a HAZOP pre-read depends on who prepared it and how much time they had; night shift gets a thinner version than day shift, and the thirtieth permit of a turnaround gets less scrutiny than the third. Silence — the worst cost is what never surfaces: the precedent incident nobody found, the safeguard that was decommissioned but still appears in the documentation, the outstanding inspection finding on the exchanger that got opened anyway. Most of these stay consequence-free. The ones that don't become incident reports. Convert the drawings once The fix is not another repository, and it is not a chatbot over the file shares. A chatbot answers questions; it does not know that PSV-201 protects V-201, or that the SOP it just retrieved references a valve that was removed two MOCs ago. The fix is to make the drawing itself smart — once. Converting scanned P&IDs into smart, connected drawings means extracting every pump, valve, line, and instrument as an object, with its connectivity, and linking each tag to the documents that describe it: datasheets, SOPs, manuals, MOCs, incidents, inspection and maintenance history, spares. One information page per asset, validated by the plant's own engineers, every link traceable to its source. After that, the tax stops compounding. The HAZOP pre-read assembles itself from the drawing and gets verified instead of built. The isolation boundary is marked on the P&ID, not traced across sheets by hand. The investigation starts from the equipment's actual history instead of a folder hunt. The first workflow takes effort. The next ten don't. This is what separates conversion from a redraw service. A manual redraw produces CAD files — accurate the day they ship, decaying from the first MOC after. Smart P&IDs with asset pages are infrastructure: every linked document, every validated correction, every completed workflow makes the base richer. The second workflow reuses the objects, source links, and review model the first one built. By the tenth, the work is being drafted from the asset base and reviewed by an engineer — instead of assembled by one. That compounding is also the honest test of any plant-AI purchase: if the second use case costs as much as the first, you bought a service, not a system. How to see the tax at your plant You don't need a study. Ask three questions about the last month. On the last MOC or HAZOP, how long did assembling the evidence take — and who did it? On the last shutdown, how much of the work-pack prep had been done before, by someone else, for a previous shutdown? When the last near-miss was investigated, was the relevant precedent found before or after the conclusions were written? If the answers are "days," "most of it," and "after," the tax is running — and it has been for years. What's new is that converting the drawings and connecting the plant's information around them is now a matter of weeks, not a multi-year services project. That is the work Raven does. If you want to see it on one of your own drawings, it takes 15 minutes. About the author Priyansh Srivastava is co-founder and CEO of Raven (YC S22). Raven converts old, scanned P&IDs into smart, connected drawings and builds one information page per asset on top — deployed in production at a 3M TPA ammonia–urea complex, where 1,000+ users work from the same validated drawings. body_text: View all news Downtown Frederick Partnership Receives $100,000 Small Business Accelerator Grant From The Hartford July 28, 2026 Download PDF (opens in new window) FREDERICK, Md., July 28, 2026 – Downtown Frederick Partnership has been awarded a $100,000 Small Business Accelerator Grant from The Hartford, in partnership with Main Street America. This grant will help launch Three’s Co., a new retail incubator in Downtown Frederick, that will help early-stage retail entrepreneurs test, grow and strengthen their businesses in a supportive, lower-risk environment. Downtown Frederick Partnership will manage the program in partnership with SOUL Street, a Frederick-based collective of Black business owners and community leaders dedicated to fostering entrepreneurial success. The shared storefront will be located in a central retail corridor within Frederick’s Main Street district. The space will support three small business owners with access for up to 12 months, offering an opportunity to build their customer base, refine operations and prepare for a permanent brick-and-mortar location. “As a leading insurer of more than one million small businesses, The Hartford understands the vital role they serve in our communities, and we are proud to go beyond the policy to support their success” said Chris Jones, head of Small Business at The Hartford. “Through our partnership with Main Street America, we are helping remove barriers to growth by expanding access to flexible, affordable accelerator spaces where entrepreneurs can build experience, reach new customers and contribute to downtown revitalization.” “Access to affordable space and accessible education can make or break a new small business,” said Matt Wagner, Chief Innovation Officer at Main Street America. “The Hartford Small Business Accelerator Program is helping Main Streets remove those barriers in real, tangible ways – and in doing so, they’re building more resilient, opportunity-rich communities for everyone. Through this program, Main Street programs are identifying the kinds of support entrepreneurs need and creating spaces that further their district’s and community’s goals.” “We’re thrilled to be opening this incubator, which advances a key goal set by the Partnership’s Business Development Committee – to cultivate new retail entrepreneurs from idea to implementation while diversifying ownership and offerings in Downtown Frederick,” said Kara Norman, Executive Director of Downtown Frederick Partnership. “It fills a critical need for affordable, accessible pathways into brick-and-mortar retail, particularly for entrepreneurs in the downtown business community.” In addition to retail space, participants will receive tailored business-development training, mentorship and networking opportunities. The program is designed to help entrepreneurs build the skills, customer base and operating experience needed to transition into sustainable, full-time storefront businesses. Downtown Frederick Partnership’s grant is part of The Hartford's multiyear, $2 million Small Business Accelerator Grant Program with Main Street America, which supports 15 communities and approximately 1,500 small businesses nationwide. About Downtown Frederick Partnership Founded in 1990, Downtown Frederick Partnership is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization dedicated to enhancing, promoting and preserving the vitality, livability and diversity of Downtown Frederick — a nationally recognized Main Street community. The Partnership has managed Downtown Frederick’s Main Street program since its designation in 2001, playing a pivotal role in downtown’s revitalization, economic growth and community engagement. Learn more at downtownfrederick.org. Downtown Frederick Partnership is one of 33 designated Main Street communities across the state of Maryland. Learn more about Main Street Maryland at mainstreetmaryland.org. About Main Street America Main Street America (MSA) leads an inclusive, impact-driven movement dedicated to reenergizing and strengthening older and historic downtowns and neighborhood commercial districts through place-based economic development and community preservation. We work in collaboration with thousands of local partners and grassroots leaders across the nation who share our commitment to advancing shared prosperity, creating resilient economies, and improving quality of life. Main Street America was founded in 1980 as the National Main Street Center®, a program of the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Over the past 40 years the MSA network has helped to generate over $115.27 billion in local reinvestment, rehab 345,801 buildings, create 815,894 new jobs, and start 181,647 new businesses in over 2,000 communities. About The Hartford The Hartford is a leader in property and casualty insurance and employee benefits. By anticipating challenges and reducing risks our customers face, the company helps people and businesses thrive with confidence. Built on a foundation of trust, The Hartford is committed to strong performance, exceptional customer experiences and bold innovation, hallmarks of its sustained success since 1810. The Hartford Insurance Group, Inc., (NYSE: HIG) operates through its subsidiaries under the brand name, The Hartford, and is headquartered in Hartford, Connecticut. More information on the company and its financial performance is available on its website. For additional details, please read The Hartford’s legal notice . title: Waxing vs. Sugaring: Which Lasts Longer and Hurts Less?
summary: By Jamie Conner, Senior Field Trainer at European Wax CenterJamie Conner trains aestheticians across European Wax Center's network on wax application technique, skin sensitivity protocols, and hygiene standards. body_text: By Jamie Conner, Senior Field Trainer at European Wax Center Jamie Conner trains aestheticians across European Wax Center's network on wax application technique, skin sensitivity protocols, and hygiene standards. She has 17 years of hands-on experience in professional hair removal. Quick Answer I get asked about sugaring almost every week, so let me answer it directly: waxing and sugaring both remove hair from the root, but in my experience, waxing typically lasts longer, works on shorter hair, and can be applied faster by a trained professional. Sugaring may suit those with very sensitive skin, but it requires longer hair growth between sessions, and I've seen results vary a lot more depending on technique. For guests seeking smooth, dependable results, I recommend professional waxing. What is Waxing? Waxing uses warm wax to adhere to hair and pull it out from the root. There are two main types: soft wax, which is removed with a cloth or paper strip, and hard wax, which hardens on the skin and is removed directly without a strip. At European Wax Center, we use Comfort Wax®, an exclusive wax formulation designed for sensitive areas like the bikini line and underarms, because it grips the hair rather than the skin. What is Sugaring? Sugaring uses a paste made from sugar, water, and lemon juice to remove hair from the root. It's applied by hand, typically against the direction of hair growth, and removed in the direction of growth. Like waxing, it pulls hair from below the skin's surface rather than just cutting it at the surface the way shaving does. Waxing vs. Sugaring: Key Differences Here's the comparison I walk new estheticians through when they ask how the two methods stack up: Waxing Sugaring Technique Cleaner, more complete removal with proper technique More technique-dependent; hair breakage can occur if the hair isn't fully removed from the root Hair length needed About 1/4 inch About 1/4 to 1/2 inch Speed per session Faster Slower Regrowth cycle Roughly 3-4 weeks Roughly 3-4 weeks, less consistent Pain level Moderate; improved with modern hard wax Moderate Hygiene/application Single-use application, no double-dipping Reusable paste ball common; varies by provider Best for Most skin types and larger areas Very sensitive skin, smaller areas Which Lasts Longer: Waxing or Sugaring? In my experience, waxing delivers longer-lasting smoothness. Sugaring involves repeated manipulation and friction during application which can sometimes cause the hair to break instead of being removed completely from the root. When that happens, regrowth may become noticeable sooner, and repeated breakage over time can contribute to ongoing irritation for some guests. As with any professional hair removal service, technique plays a significant role in the final result. Is Sugaring Less Painful Than Waxing? This is probably the question I field most often, and my honest answer is: pain levels are more similar than people assume. The idea that sugaring "hurts less" usually traces back to comparisons with old-style soft wax from years ago. The hard wax formulation I train on today is built to grip hair, not skin, which cuts down on discomfort significantly compared to older techniques. In my experience, comfort has much more to do with technique and formulation than with which method you choose. Which Is Better for Sensitive Skin? Both can work well for sensitive skin when done correctly. Sugaring paste is applied at body temperature, and some guests do find that gentler on reactive skin. That said, European Wax Center’s Comfort Wax, the hard wax formulation we use, is specifically built to minimize irritation on sensitive areas, and as a trainer, I can adjust technique and aftercare guidance to reduce redness or bumps for nearly any skin type. I don't hesitate to recommend professional waxing even for guests with sensitive skin because when the hair is removed cleanly from the root instead of breaking, there’s typically less need to repeatedly work over the same area. Is Waxing More Hygienic Than Sugaring? From a hygiene standpoint, professional waxing has a real edge when protocols are followed closely which is something I'm strict about in training. At European Wax Center, every guest gets new single-use applicators for each dip, and we never double-dip into the wax pot. Traditional sugaring often involves one reusable paste ball worked by hand across the skin, which carries a higher risk of cross-contamination if proper protocols aren't strictly maintained between clients. Health and hygiene standards are a non-negotiable at European Wax Center. Why Choose Professional Waxing? After years of training on technique, formulation, and hygiene protocol, my honest recommendation is professional waxing for most guests. Waxing typically provides more consistent, longer-lasting smoothness when performed by a trained, certified esthetician using our exclusive Comfort Wax formulation and standardized protocols to deliver results you can count on, visit after visit, location after location. Frequently Asked Questions Is waxing or sugaring better? Waxing is generally the better choice for most people because it lasts longer, works on shorter hair, and is faster to apply professionally. Sugaring can suit those with very sensitive skin or a preference for simpler ingredients. Is waxing more hygienic than sugaring? Yes, in most professional settings. Waxing services like European Wax Center use single-use applicators for every client, while traditional sugaring often relies on a reusable paste ball that carries a higher risk of cross-contamination if hygiene protocols aren't strictly followed. Does sugaring hurt less than waxing? Not necessarily. Pain levels are similar between the two methods, and modern hard wax formulations have significantly reduced the discomfort once associated with waxing. How long does sugaring last compared to waxing? Both methods offer regrowth cycles of roughly 3–4 weeks, but waxing tends to produce more consistent, complete hair removal, which can extend the time before regrowth becomes noticeable. Can you switch from sugaring to waxing? Yes. As long as hair has reached the minimum length needed for waxing (about 1/4 inch), you can switch between methods without issue. Is sugaring more natural than waxing? Sugaring paste is made from simple ingredients like sugar, water, and lemon juice. However, "natural" ingredients don't necessarily mean better results as modern wax formulations are designed with skin compatibility and effectiveness in mind, often offering superior outcomes for most guests.
